musculoskeletal.label: Musculoskeletal condition (muscle / tendon / joint related)
evidence_notes: Pain that increases with activity/movement and improves with rest is commonly associated with musculoskeletal strain.
Localized tenderness over a single muscle group is a typical musculoskeletal pattern.
Gradual onset without numbness/tingling lowers likelihood of nerve involvement.
guidance: Relative rest of the affected area, avoiding movements that sharply worsen pain
Gentle stretching and gradual return to activity as tolerated
Consult a physiotherapist or orthopedic specialist if pain persists beyond 2-3 weeks

peripheral_nerve.label: Peripheral nerve involvement
evidence_notes: Numbness or tingling following a specific nerve distribution pattern suggests possible nerve involvement.
Weakness accompanied by sensory changes (numbness/tingling) raises suspicion for nerve-related causes rather than pure muscle strain.
Symptoms worsened by specific postures (e.g., sitting, bending) can indicate nerve compression.
guidance: Avoid prolonged pressure or positions that reproduce symptoms
Track whether numbness/tingling is spreading or constant
Neurological evaluation (neurologist) is recommended for confirmation and nerve conduction studies if needed

neuromuscular.label: Neuromuscular condition (nerve-muscle junction / motor pathway)
evidence_notes: Progressive (worsening over weeks) weakness rather than fluctuating pain is a pattern seen in neuromuscular conditions.
Weakness that worsens with repeated activity/fatigue through the day is a notable pattern warranting evaluation.
Balance or coordination difficulty alongside weakness increases relevance of neuromuscular evaluation.
guidance: Do not ignore progressive weakness - clinical evaluation is important
Keep a symptom diary noting time of day and activity level
Neurologist evaluation with possible EMG/nerve conduction studies is the appropriate next step

vascular.label: Vascular contribution (blood flow related)
evidence_notes: Cramping pain that appears after a consistent walking distance and resolves with rest can indicate a vascular pattern (claudication).
Skin color or temperature changes in the affected limb add relevance to vascular causes.
guidance: Note the exact walking distance that triggers symptoms and how long rest takes to relieve it
Avoid smoking/tobacco if applicable, as it affects circulation
Vascular or general physician evaluation is recommended

emergency.label: Potential emergency / urgent presentation
typical_symptoms: loss of bladder or bowel control
evidence_notes: Sudden onset of severe weakness or numbness, especially one-sided, is a recognized red-flag pattern.
Loss of bladder or bowel control alongside limb weakness is a recognized red-flag combination.
Rapid worsening over hours (rather than days/weeks) is treated as a red flag in clinical screening.
guidance: Do not wait for routine appointment scheduling
Contact emergency services or go to the nearest emergency department
